sentences.text: Psittacosaurus is a genus of extinct ceratopsian dinosaurs known as the "parrot lizard" in Greek.
It is the most species-rich non-avian dinosaur genus, with up to 13 known species.
Currently, between nine and eleven species are considered valid out of seventeen that have been referred to the genus.
This genus holds the record for the highest number of valid species assigned to any single non-avian dinosaur genus.
All species were gazelle-sized, bipedal herbivores with a high and powerful beak on the upper jaw.
Henry Fairfield Osborn participated in the 1922 Third Asiatic Expedition of the American Museum of Natural History in Mongolia.
A Mongolian chauffeur named Wong discovered a nearly complete skeleton nicknamed the "Red Mesa skeleton".
The holotype specimen AMNH 6254 was described by Osborn in 1924 and named Psittacosaurus mongoliensis.
Osborn distinguished the animal by its short deep snout, broad rear skull, and lack of teeth in the premaxilla.
Adult Psittacosaurus were obligate bipeds characterized by a high skull and a robust beak.
Researchers suggest Psittacosaurus had complex behaviors based on its brain proportions and size.
The animal may have been active during both day and night and possessed well-developed senses of smell and vision.
Protiguanodon and Hongshanosaurus are synonyms of Psittacosaurus.
The generic name Hongshanosaurus is derived from the Chinese words for "red" and "hill" combined with the Greek word for "lizard".
The genus Psittacosaurus was named by Osborn in 1923.
The type species of the genus is Psittacosaurus mongoliensis.
Psittacosaurus lived between 125 and 105 million years ago.
Fossils have been found in Asia during the Early Cretaceous period.
The Oshih locality where Psittacosaurus was found dates to the Early Cretaceous Aptian to Albian age.
Psittacosaurus mongoliensis fossils are found in strata dating to the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 to 100 million years ago.
Paul Sereno questioned the validity of P. sattayaraki in 2000 due to its eroded and fragmentary nature and lack of characteristic Psittacosaurus features.
In 2002, the original authors of P. sattayaraki published new images showing teeth with a bulbous vertical ridge characteristic of psittacosaurs, defending the species' validity.
In 2010, Paul Sereno proposed that the type material of P. sattayaraki might best be assigned to Ceratopsia incertae sedis.
Paul Sereno found P. ordosensis indistinguishable from P. sinensis in 2010 but suggested further study might reveal diagnostic features.
